utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are Thursday today, and we are running 10 minutes late through no fault of mine. We are starting the hearing. I would like to thank everybody present in and around the courtroom. I should like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, of the Defence team, as well as all the people present. Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I wonder if that would be a proper time to introduce -- to tender the documents in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you drawn up a list of documents? Very well. We have a list here. So we shall discuss it between us and rule on it at a later stage. We shall now move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness BJ, you were then assigned to the Tactical Group Canarias, which was part of the Spanish army Rapid Action Force when you were deployed to Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it is correct, sir, that your first time in Bosnia-Herzegovina was as part of a reconnaissance mission in March of 1993, and you arrived for your permanent duty, or your mission duty at that time, on approximately the 20th of April, 1993, in Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19th of April, not 20. I heard 29th, but I arrived on the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And you and your group, the Canarias group, were then deployed in this mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina until October, 1993, and perhaps if you recall you can give us the particular date of that as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that we arrived 30th of September or 1st of October. We arrived in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, can you tell the Judges now -- describe briefly what the mission or mandate of the Spanish Battalion, the peacekeeping -- the UNPROFOR peacekeeping force known as Spanish Battalion, or as I'm sure we'll hear in the course of the day SpaBat, can you tell the Judges what the mission or mandate of SpaBat was during this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The task was to escort humanitarian aid convoys when they came under our AOR on the defence of people, UN personnel in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say OA -- AOR, excuse me, for the purpose of the record, does that mean area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the answer you gave a moment ago, were there times when the Spanish Battalion or its senior officers became -- also became involved in various negotiations related to peace agreements or cease-fire negotiations between, for example, the HVO and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did participate in talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were there also times when you participated, not you personally necessarily, but that SpaBat participated in such things as body exchanges between the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did participate in the exchange of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I think you may be the first officer from UNPROFOR that has appeared in the trial so far, so I'll ask you a couple of questions about UNPROFOR. Can you tell the Judges where the headquarters for all of UNPROFOR was based in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Where was that located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The general headquarters of UNPROFOR in Bosnia-Herzegovina was in Kiseljak, and there was also a detachment in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The main operational headquarters was in Kiseljak; is that correct? Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the AOR a moment ago. Can you tell the Judges, during the time of the SpaBat's mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you tell the Judges what your area of responsibility, or the battalion's area of responsibility was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the Metkovic area in Croatia and all along the road arriving in Mostar to a village known as Kontic on the West M Prolog.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance. I think most of the documents will be in e-court. If we could maybe bend the ELMO apparatus down a bit so I can see the witness. Thank you so much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges, please, the locations, the principal locations where the Spanish Battalion had its bases of operation or outpost, but the specific more or less permanent locations that you had.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Spaniards were deployed first in Croatia, in Split, which was the logistics area; in Dracevac, which is where the Spanish Battalion was; in Medjugorje we had forces; and in Srebrenica [as interpreted] we also had some forces but we were active mostly around Mostar area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was the headquarters and the military police component of the Spanish Battalion primarily located at Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did the Spanish Battalion have a -- a more or less permanent post in or in the vicinity of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some 150 to 200 men.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, Judge. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to make a correction in the text. I believe the witness mentioned Jablanica and not Srebrenica. In the text it is Srebrenica. So it should be corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, is that correct? The transcript may have said Srebrenica. Did you in fact refer to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, did you -- did there come a time the Spanish Battalion also had a regular presence in the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't have a permanent detachment, but for almost four months we had some forces in the city, in the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just before moving forward then and off the topic of the Spanish Battalion's area of responsibility, can I just confirm with you then, as it related to this case, that the Spanish Battalion's area of responsibility included such areas as the municipality of Mostar and Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Also Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Capljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Stolac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stolac was a point for talks when we came in contact with the Serbs. The village was just on the border of the AOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Citluk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, as you -- as you and the Spanish Battalion learned that you were being sent, being tasked to Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you tell the Judges, please, what sort of orientation or training you and the battalion received in preparation for the mission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the previous six months another unit had been deployed and it sent information about what was going on in the area. We, over a month, were detached to Almeria in order to prepare the Bosnia-Herzegovina mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges a bit more about what sort of training or information you received during this training or transition period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were provided with information, with documentary information produced by the Malaga group. We received this in the Almeria headquarters, and we perused all the information contained therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you made a point that perhaps I should clarify or make clear to the Chamber. Your group, the Canarias group, was not the first contingent of the Spanish army in the UNPROFOR force, but there was also a force called the Malaga group, or force, prior to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Malaga Tactical Group was deployed six months before then. The Canarias detachment was sent, and then we ourselves were then followed by the Madrid group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So in sequence, those are the three components of the Spanish army that performed as part of the peacekeeping operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was another group, if I'm not mistaken, but it was when the change from UNPROFOR to NATO took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to talk about then the structure of the Spanish Battalion during its operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and for the moment when I talk about these positions, sir, I'll ask you not to mention the individual names of officers or Spanish Battalion personnel but simply to -- we'll talk about these things in terms of their position. If we get to a point where a specific name appears to be necessary or appropriate, then we will go in private session, or at least I'll ask to go into private session. Is it correct, sir, that the Spanish Battalion, the command structure was divided into approximately five sections or working groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not the command, the advisors to the heads of the association, the advisors were five. The colonel staff [as interpreted], that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There was a section called S1, I believe, and the section S1, was that involved with personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there a section S2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And had to do with information and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, I'm going to caution you on this. I'll caution you again not to mention any names at this particular point, but was there also a section S3?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the section S4, what was the name and function of that section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Logistics for our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we go further, if we could have -- if I could please request that the portion in which the witness identified -- which he said was a part, if that could be-

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, being a bit systematic, as we have five sections, could I ask what S5 would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was going to get to that. I can do it now and perhaps we can go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was premature. It's your interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. My only point was to say could we please have the part where the witness said -- referred to his part, on line 24, page 20, redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, could you tell us, then, was there also a section called S5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Civilian affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What kinds of operations or functions were they involved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you asking me in relation to S5? Contact with the parties involved, contact with the civilian personnel and with the organisations of humanitarian aid and non-government organisations, relations with the United Nations, relations with the organisations for refugees, and also contacts for -- in relation to vehicles. Contacts in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar. Yes, please give an order for the request just made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could in that regard also go into private session just for a few moments, please, to talk about the witness's specific function, which would tend to identify him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell the Judges, given these five sections, what -- how they operated together. What was the flow of information and reporting from one section to another and to the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day there was a coordination meeting where we all met, all the sections, with the chief of staff who coordinated all the sections. We all reported in terms of information we had to report on, and we also coordinated basically what had to be done throughout day in terms of operations movements or searches for information or any other matters that we needed to attend to. Normally, the S3 and S2 worked together. It was a group that worked closely, intimately. We were in constant contact, and we also worked together with S4. We worked together always, and S5 cooperated and worked with both groups, and there was a series of negotiations and we had been given a number of information reports which had been circulated from one section to another as well as a series of information reports that was circulated among the various sections not only in terms of logistics but also in terms of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record -- it was just corrected. Thank you. Just a correction in the transcript. Sir, you just mentioned the reports that were shared or circulated among the various sections, and that was exactly my next topic. Is it correct that as part of the Spanish Battalion's operations during this time, as I understand it there were three principal types of records or reports that were made, and I'll -- I'm going to ask you about these in more detail, but the first one was called an intrep; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. Intrep, a report on intelligence or intelligence report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which of the sections would prepare an intrep generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My section was in charge of preparing the report, the situation report. Sitrep, situation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll ask for the correction of line 2, the redaction to "my section." Let me let me just direct your attention, Witness, specifically again to the intrep first. Which section was specifically responsible for preparing that particular report, the intrep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Section 2. Section 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were those reports prepared on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. There were daily reports, and they were addressed to all the command posts in Spain as well as the rest of other units of the Spanish Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the typical time of day that the intrep for that day, if you will, would typically be issued or completed and put out, if you will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would change, but as a rule that would be towards the end of the day, around 7.00 or 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to go on to another report. Was there also something called the intsum? What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't intersum, it's intsum. It was a report, it was a summary of specific points that were not on a regular basis. They could be on a regular basis every week or every two weeks and they were in relation to concrete items and often there were situation reports or intelligence reports which would come from command posts all the way down to us. And that was in relation to specific points, not general items.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did the S3 section produce a report called a sitrep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. On a daily basis, towards the end of the afternoon, we would produce a report in relation to the situation of the Spanish Battalion at that time or what operations we had foreseen for the rest of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that was again a report that was issued essentially at the end of each mission day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. Towards the end of the afternoon, and also it would be addressed to the same correspondents, the chiefs of staff as well as UNPROFOR and the heads of the battalions and the advisors of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. So just by way of a quick summary, we have the intrep or what we might call the intelligence report, intsum or intelligence summary, and the sitrep or situation report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've made references to this already but I wanted to be a bit more specific on this. When each of these reports were prepared, can you tell the Judges what the circulation of these reports to -- excuse me, were, what the circulation was, I suppose I should say, what the circulation was, not only internal to the Spanish Battalion but where these reports might have gone outside the immediate Spanish Battalion headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All these reports in terms of intrep and sitrep, they were addressed to the chiefs of staff in Spain, to the chiefs of UNPROFOR, and also they were distributed to all the subordinate sections in the battalion, the different companies, the sapper units, and the chiefs of staff of the 4th, 5th division, and other advisors of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, and again with the understanding that it will not be broadcast outside the courtroom, can I have the assistance display to the witness and to those in court Exhibit P 03018.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we are going to find it difficult to find our way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. It is in the two smaller -- let me say for the record there are two, if you will, relatively speaking, smaller binders of tabbed exhibits that specifically will be used with the witness and then there's the larger collection of binders containing all of the selected Spanish Battalion material, and I am now looking in the bundle of exhibits. The top one is 2481. The documents are arranged numerically. And we're looking now at Exhibit 3018.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, can you see -- you have that document before you now in the Spanish language, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just -- the reason I'm showing you this document, sir, is so you can explain to the Judges just in general terms, not as a specific point of information, this particular document. Can you tell the Judges what this particular document, what type of document this is of the ones we discussed a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a fax message which had been sent to a number of addressees, the intrep. Here I cannot see the number. Maybe scroll down. And that is dated the 30th of June. To whom it was addressed and all the relevant stamps in relation to receipt and exit, the PDC receipt, which is the control tab for confidential documentation, and this is a typical document of the Spanish Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would this document -- you just said -- for the purposes so the record is very clear, would this document, in your view, be typical or representative of a document that you have described today as a sitrep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in -- not concretely this one in particular. It's not a sitrep. But the -- the cover page will be very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I misspoke, Witness. My fault. Would this be representative of an intrep document that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I could just ask you to briefly cast your eyes over the -- at least on the English version the -- what would appear to be the bottom half of the first page, where it indicates the from, the to, information, and would you just look at that and, generally speaking, say is that again -- would that be typical or representative of the distribution of such a report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. It was sent by the chief of the group, and it was addressed to the different chiefs, the chiefs of sappers, of logistics, of explosives, and other units. And also, these type of documents, when they may be of interest to other parties, they are included and it is explained for their knowledge without any further action required. And they could be different chiefs within the army or other groups of the EGM -- JEME, rather, that could be in relation to chiefs of press matters. And also S1, S2, S3, S4, S5 were also parties in relation to the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Could I ask the witness next to be shown Exhibit P 02235, and for Your Honours it will be in -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. As we are going to be talking about these documents, I'd just like to clarify one point. In this document, in Spanish we can read "fiabilidad" and "credibilidad." We see C-2, credibility and reliability. Is there a scale as far as reliability and credibility is concerned? If that is the case, could you tell us what kind of scale is used. I'm talking about the document that would be the most reliable to the document that would be the least reliable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The garners [as interpreted] go from 1 to 6. The first one is in relation to whether the news item is reliable or not. The second number, from 1 to 6, in terms of A, B, C, D, the second one would be in relation to numbers 1 to 6 and relates to the reliability of the source of the information. And the highest reliability or the highest and most reliable information would be a 6, and the least one would be a 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document we can see -- we see C-2 reliability, which is just the opposite to what you just said. Reliability is represented in terms of figures and credibility in terms of letters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The letters relate to credibility of the news, of the information, and the number is the credibility or reliability of the source. So whether it's reliability, credibility, it's in relation to the news or source, the person who is issuing the news or the information, and also in relation to whether the news or the information is accurate or incorrect or inaccurate. So it goes both in relation to news and source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant is this -- perhaps we could have a closer look at the document, please. Could you show this document on the screen, please, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have the report -- the document on screen. It has been removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is -- it's not the first page, it's the second page, and we can see that there's "Confidential" written on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I see on one -- on e-court, at least the screen that the Prosecution is looking at [Spanish on English channel]. If we can go on to a further page somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have page 59, 29, and 99.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We should be able to go forward. It seems to ... We can put it on the ELMO then, I suppose. Again, it won't -- not to be broadcast outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Actually, it can be shown to the witness, I suppose, if he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put it on the ELMO so that everyone can see it, please. So here we have it. If you could look at the fourth line, "Reliability/credibility: C-2." So reliability is expressed in terms of letters and credibility in terms of figures; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Affirmative. Affirmative. But in relations to -- reliability in relation to news and in terms of credibility, that goes in relation to the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the source is number 2, and reliability is the letter C, whereas you said that you referred to A, B, C and D. So when looking at these documents, we need to look at this more specifically. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could next go to -- then to Exhibit P 02235. I will try to do it electronically, but -- if we can. And it will be in the -- that document will be in the other of the two bundles, again in numerical order. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot see it. I cannot see it. Now I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Will you please look at that for a moment, and can you tell the Judges, is this particular document representative of the type of document that you've indicated or identified this morning as a sitrep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is a typical sitrep document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, looking at that, such things as the distribution, the format of the document, type of information reported, if you need to look further, but again, this would be representative of such a document in general; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is enough, thank you. This document, while I haven't really seen the distribution, distribution is only to the higher echelons, to the command post. It's not showing whether it's going to any lower units. This being said, the answer to your question whether this is representative is yes. If you can lower it down a little bit so I can see the rest of it. Thank you. No, no. A little bit higher. I made a mistake. Stop it there. Thank you. Yes. We see in this document this one is only to be distributed to the command post Comfar in Spain, not to the lower units on the spot. For this one particular document, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Unless the Judges have a particular -- we'll be looking at a number of these kinds of documents, but unless the Judges have a question on this particular document, I'll move on. Sir, can you, in addition to the three reports that we've briefly covered now - and we'll see a number of those in the course of the next few hours, I believe - was it part of the official record-keeping of the Spanish Battalion that there was also something called the diary of operations or logbook of operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. Yes. The third section did have a logbook of operations or a diary of operations, as we would call it in Spanish, where we recorded the history of the unit, the day-to-day history of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the registry's assistance, please, to display Exhibit P 01717. And, Your Honours, that will be the first document in one of the two bundles. 01717. If we could let the witness see a bit more of the document possibly, or maybe reduce the size. Maybe if we can get a page, maybe, at a time. Could we show him the first several pages, possibly? Can we leaf through the first couple of pages, if possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly recognise this operations logbook. It is the operations logbook of the Spanish Battalion at the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, from having looked at this document and, in transparency, not just at this particular moment but when you reviewed this document over the past several days, can you confirm to the Judges that this is the operations logbook or diary of the Spanish Battalion unit during its tour of operations from approximately the middle of April until October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. The answer affirmative. This is the operations logbook of the Canarias group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, if we look at the document, there may be a few entries that predate back, it appears to be, as to the latter part of March; is that correct? If the witness could be shown, for example, approximately the third page of the document. You see an entry, sir, for the 29th of March, 1993, by example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can direct -- if it's possible for the registry to please go to the end of that document, the very last page of that document, and for the Chamber to the last page of the hard copy. As soon as you have -- sir, can you tell us, and again without -- there is no reason in particular at this moment to mention the person by name, but when you look at the bottom of the last page of the log, does it bear the signature of the commanding officer of that group at the end -- at the approximate end of the tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. Affirmative. Yes, that is the big chief of the Canarias group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, this operations logbook, we don't seem to have the translation into English, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You should have it. I think Your Honours have both. In fact, in this particular document I believe you have both the Spanish and the English. Your Honour, looking at the clock, and I'm about to change topics, if this might be the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is now time to have a break. We shall have a 20-minute break and resume at five minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, may I just indicate to the Court that at a convenient time, whenever this can conveniently be done, may I have about two or three minutes to address Your Honours on the subject of the admissibility of the documents that were produced yesterday by the witness Mr. Hujdur. That's a matter which Your Honours have not yet ruled on. I would just like to speak to it at some convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We'll do that at the end of the sitting. Let's resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the registry's assistance by going next to Exhibit P 02192.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could just look at that document, and if you can see enough of it, and you'll just have to assist us, please, if you need to see another part of the document, you may have to tell us what you need to see. Can you tell us, is this an intrep, number 162, dated approximately the 4th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could refer -- if I could ask the -- that the witness be shown in the Spanish document pages 3 and 4. And on the English version, for those looking at the English version, page 4. And for the section referencing Jablanica. It just may assist, since people are looking at different versions -- I think we just had it a moment ago. Okay. Some part of it carries over, I see, on the Spanish page. The document refers, it appears, to a meeting, an escort going towards Sovici and Doljani and provided for a number of people, Generals Halilovic and Pasalic, Petkovic, and Basic, SpaBat's commanding officer, and others. Towards the end of that particular entry, if you see, it says the following, and I'll ask you a couple of questions about this: "The town of Doljani, utterly destroyed and torched, was the first place to be visited. On leaving this locality, some women indicated that all the men had been taken to Sovici. Later Sovici was visited where some 60 elderly men were being detained in the school building." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do see it. I see the document and this is a document issued by the Canarias group, and the information given there is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I intervene at this point? The witness says the information is correct. No hesitation. If we look at the title, we find again C-2 as to credibility. On page 2, the fourth line. And that is relatively low. There seems to be a contrast between what you affirm, Colonel, and this classification. We've had it before already. Is it -- is it routine that you put in C-2 here, or how could you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I could explain. Perhaps there's a routine aspect involved, but we speaking about a whole document. I'm not speaking about a specific trip to Doljani or to Sovici. We're speaking about the whole of the document wherein much more information is concerned. So regarding all of the information concerned in the document, it only rates a C-2, not the specific bit of the visit to these towns. We hardly ever get maximum reliability and credibility in any document. Hardly ever. We never -- I don't think we ever gave a document an A-6 top credibility and reliability rating. In this case it got a C-2 no doubt because there were other elements of information which were not as credible as this particular one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, following on from that, then, may I ask that it should be made clear in relation to each of these documents what the level of reliability and credibility may be as to each item that Mr. Scott asks about and not about just the whole document generically, because one matter that Your Honours are going to have to decide at a later time is the probative value of these documents, or to put that another way, what rating on the numerical and alphabetical scale amounts to proof beyond reasonable doubt, and it's important, I think, to have an evaluation of the facts Mr. Scott is asking about and not just a generic evaluation of the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I may make some inquiries, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we've asked the question, then we realise the importance of it. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we go to the specific question raised by counsel, Witness, which I assume you've heard and we'll come to in a moment, in terms of the ranking system, let just me make sure that I understood correctly. I don't have the transcript from earlier in front of me now. The alphabetical references, the references A through F, or whatever you mentioned -- excuse me, may have mentioned earlier, is the A the higher -- the highest of the grade and then going down from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in terms of the numerical references, is it also similar that number 1 represents the most reliable information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So the reference just so we're all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is in contrast to what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. It's the other way around. I made a mistake. The other way around in numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So when you say "the other way around" again, for the very reason that Judge Trechsel has indicated, that's why I want to be very clear. So when you say "the other way around," are you saying that number 6 is the highest rating or number 1 is the highest rating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 6 is the highest credibility rating, sir. I repeat: 6 is the highest credibility rating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the highest rating we could possibly get, if I understand the system correctly, would be an A-6. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. That would mean a really true fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And stating the converse, so again that we're all on the same page, the lowest possible rating would be an F-1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: F-1 indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. While we're dealing with this issue, I would like the witness to tell us when it comes to reliability and credibility, reliability is - as far as I understood it, but I might be wrong - the origin, the source providing the information, and credibility is the value attributed to the contents. Is that correct or not? Could you tell us the difference once again between reliability and credibility. What is related to source and what is related to content?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's an opposite of what you have said, the opposite. Reliability is the reliability of the news itself, the news item itself. That is reliability, whether the news is true or false, whether it's really reliable. Credibility is the credibility of the source of the news, whether or not we can trust the source from which that news item emerges or is emitted. This is what I said earlier, and this is what I am now repeating, sir. Credibility source, reliability news. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will keep that definition, although one could think differently, but we're going to stick to your definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, let me next turn to a question that was raised a few moments ago. The practice of the Spanish Battalion was to give this rating to the overall -- to the report as a whole, if I understood your testimony a few minutes ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't really understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. The question was raised in reference to the rating, and in this particular instance let me make sure that I'm also looking at the correct document myself. 02192, we have a reference to a C-2. You have that -- if you can see that part of the document. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I understand the point that was being made earlier, please correct me if I'm wrong, that this rating relates to the document as a whole, the information contained in the document as a whole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there any place on this document that you can show us on this document where the individual items or the individual entries were rated separately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I really don't know what you're driving at. Are you driving to a specific part of the document, a specific element of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. If we looked, for example, as to any entry in the document, if you look to the section on Konjic, for instance, on page 5 of the English version -- I saw it a moment ago in the Spanish version, but if you can find the section on Konjic. It's one that catches my eye at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Page 4 of the Spanish version. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is there anything that you can -- is there any rating in the document that tells us -- any rating as to the credibility and reliability of that specific piece of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm very much afraid that I did not draft that particular intrep. I don't know what the sources are. As I did not draft this document, I cannot tell you what the rating would be, whether this is a truth or a falsehood. I do remember having read this document at the time. I may have an opinion of myself -- myself, but it's just an opinion. It's very subjective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... little bit more specific. Under letter (b) in Konjic, there is a reference to a patrol of SpaBat which heard, I think, members of the mixed commission. I guess, but it's for you to tell me, that the credibility and the quality of the source when it is one of your own patrols is better than C-2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There can be no doubt if the information comes from one of us who was present at the time, then reliability is total. For instance, if there is a SpaBat patrol that actually carried out something in that particular action, that information is totally correct. But the paragraph underneath speaks about some local information, you see. And whether or not that is true, whether or not it is correct, we don't know. That is a local source, and I cannot actually tell you how credible it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think, then, it is justified to conclude that the general assessment of the credibility and viability of the document is of rather little value because it does not make sense to give a global level of credibility to a document which has such diverse pieces of information. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can be quite right, but that just happens to be the regulation system in our army. It is very difficult to rate news item per news item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I just want to add, if I may, one thing to that, and that is that even with respect to information coming from a SpaBat patrol, I would ask that the Prosecution find out from this witness in any particular case whether what he's saying is based on his own personal knowledge or whether he's merely indicating that he thinks the document's reliable because an entry has been made in this report. It may be, Your Honour, that the practice -- I don't seek to attack the practice in drafting military reports. They have their own uses in the field, but when they are offered as evidence, then we have to look at them in an entirely different light, and I would ask that the Prosecution, if they are seeking to introduce these documents in evidence, at least elicit that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we're going to continue to engage in this discussion, I would ask that we excuse the witness from the courtroom. I believe now we're getting into matters of evidence and law which I disagree with counsel, but if we're going to engage in a lengthy discussion of this then we should excuse the witness and go on for an hour or two, go on for an hour or two talking about what the evidence requires, rules of evidence require.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: It's not my intention to engage in a lengthy discussion. There are some general issues that do arise, and on Monday, as Your Honour knows, the Defence has been working on a response in a somewhat different context to documents offered by the Prosecution on another occasion when they made written submissions to the Court and Your Honours said that we might have the opportunity to respond. That response will be filed on Monday, and it will address not only the documents which were then in question but certain more general issues of evidence, and it may be that that would be the appropriate time to have this discussion. I don't want to take up the time of the Court now, but these are matters which we will have to get into at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're not going to broach an in-depth discussion now, and it's been a question that's been discussed over the 10 years that the Tribunal has been in existence. We have the cross-examination, which will allow us to test allegations made in a document. There are also direct questions, that method, direct questions from the Prosecution, and the Defence can at any time say that such-and-such a document is of no value and can ask it to be rejected. But let's wait and see before we draw our conclusions. We've just started the examination-in-chief conducted by the Prosecution, so let's not make any definite conclusions at this stage. The Judges asked a few questions in order to establish the value and importance of letters and figures for reliability and credibility. We heard the answer, and we'll draw the appropriate conclusions in due course. Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In reference to the fact -- the report about the situation in Doljani and Sovici, can you just give the Chamber an idea as to when this information would be reported, say at the end of the day or at the next morning briefing, how would that sort of information affect, if any, what the Spanish Battalion do -- would do in its day-to-day operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This type of information is usually given in a document when the chief of SpaBat goes back to headquarters and reports on what has happened, where he has been, what has taken place. The influence that may have on the operations run by the Spanish Battalion is very minimal because the Spanish Battalion has specific concrete missions to carry out. When he was there, he wasn't allowed to go out looking for intelligence or for news, weather reports. It had its own very specific missions to carry out. What it tried to do was to make sure that the various parties could sit together around the same table, because we managed to get this, they wouldn't fight each other, but otherwise, it would have absolutely influence on our specific missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In this particular mission, if I understand the entry correctly and the information immediately above the reference to Doljani and Sovici, as part of this operation, if you will, or what was done that day, that involved the SpaBat commanding officer; is that correct? Again, you need not mention the person by name, but according to this report, the commanding officer was involved; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. He attended the meeting. He visited the towns mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to next -- for the registry next to go to Exhibit P 02081. If I can refer you particularly to -- I believe it may be on page 4 of the English document, and it may carry over from page 1 to page 2 of the Spanish document. The reference concerning Mostar. If you'd find that, please. This is an intrep on the 25th of April, 1993. Sir, can you find the language where it says "In Mostar fighting --" the entry fighting. "There were minor skirmishes during the night and some shots were fired during the day, however joint mission patrols supported by UNPROFOR continued to keep the situation under control." Going on down below, it says: "The headquarters of the BH army has been moved to the quarter of Mahala." The -- there's a reference in this document to joint commission patrols. Can you tell the Judges, what was a joint commission patrol at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An agreement was reached to try and keep dialogue alive, to organise patrolling in the city of Mostar with representatives of armija and of HVO, and there was also Spanish officials. And these patrols went all around the city, checked on the situation, see -- tried to identify problems, movements of population, et cetera, checkpoints at some crossroads, et cetera, and particularly when there was a problem, they immediately rushed to where people said a problem had occurred. It was essential to try to obtain information. All three parties involved, the two warring ones and SpaBat together, to try and ascertain really what was going on in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, and if you so can you tell the Chamber generally, by the end of April, early part of May, 1993, what was the status of freedom of movement, if you will, both for the SpaBat or UNPROFOR and also for the public in general? What was the status of being able to move freely around the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When these dates you mentioned, April, circulation was practically entirely free, both for UNPROFOR and SpaBat, and the civilian population totally freely. When they approached us, they greeted us, they talked to us. Although you could feel the tension in the air obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did that freedom of movement change over time as your tour of duty continued? And tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the situation did change when there was attack in Mostar in -- towards the Muslim area. And then in the Bulevar area there was widespread fighting, and then people stopped circulating around Mostar. Only within their own limited neighbourhoods, but there was no exchange between them, and the Spanish units were withdrawn to the west of the city, to the hospital area, from which we could dominate the city. We had quite a view of the whole of the city but we were outside the confrontation area. We were told by the Croats that combat was about to begin and for our own security we had to withdraw. Now, our mission would have been obviously to try and maintain peace, but we did have to withdraw our units to continue observation from a secure post.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll talk about some of those points you just made in a few moments. Could I ask you to next look at Exhibit P 02220. And I believe the entry that I'll refer -- I'll refer you to is on page 3 of the English version and perhaps pages 2 carrying over to page 3 of the Spanish version. And this is intrep number 165, apparently dated the 7th of May, 1993. The 7th or the 8th. You can assist us on that. Do you have that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to look at the page reference that I just mentioned a moment ago. I believe it will be on pages 2 to 3 of your -- of the Spanish original. Can you see the language where it says: "The HVO CP in the vicinity of Konjic is still blocking the passage of all except the UNPROFOR vehicles"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For the record, can you say -- can you tell the Judges what the reference "CP" refers to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Checkpoint. That means checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can please direct your attention a bit further on in the document, not too far but a bit further on where there's reference to Mostar. Do you see the language: "The captain of the company serving in the city received reports from HVO and BiH in which they accused each other for failing to comply with conditions of the agreement that both parties had signed"? And then continuing on down: "Comment. The situation has deteriorated to the extent that an open conflict seems to be unavoidable, which perhaps hasn't happened yet because of the tranquillising presence of the SpaBat units." Two questions. When it refers to the company -- excuse me, the captain of the company, are you referring to the captain of the Spanish Battalion company that was operating in Mostar at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. There was a permanent company. In our joint commission there's a company that was patrolling in the whole of the city on the command of a captain who belonged to the joint commission together with the other two parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, it makes reference to the "tranquillising presence of the Spanish Battalion units." Can you give the Judges again some further sense of what the Spanish Battalion was doing around the 7th or 8th of May in terms of trying to, if you will, keep things peaceful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, basically our order was not actually to impose peace on anybody, but we tried to remain in that area, to be present at crossroads, to be visible around the city, to reassure the civilian population that we were not abandoning them, that they could count on us if need be. But actually being able to do things, there was very little we were able to do. But it was mostly being present and visible to reassure people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to have an explanation to evaluate what you're saying. We're speaking about the 8th and 9th of May, 1993. Now, your office, where was it physically? Where were you, physically speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Thank you. And did you go to Mostar from time to time to see with your own eyes what the situation was like in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did go to Mostar couple of times, on the 7th and 8th, or 8th and 9th, I'm not sure. But I did habitually go and I tried to visit the company there detached because we had some contacts with the HVO headquarters, or the armija headquarters. I was there a couple of times, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation in the city was, as I said before, tense. But the civilian population welcomed us. They came to us, brought us coffee. They smiled at us, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for giving me that explanation. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I heard you correctly, and the transcript -- at least the live transcript we're getting has moved off that information now -- but if I heard you correctly a few minutes ago, you said that there came some information from the HVO that the Spanish Battalion or its component in Mostar should leave the area or take some action because of fighting that was anticipated. Can you tell the Judges more, please, specifically about that. What information was received from the Spanish Battalion and when was that, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the night in which the fighting broke out in Mostar, the patrol -- part of the patrol were near bridges near the conflict area and the separation area between Croats and Muslims. That night the officers in charge of the patrols were approached by HVO members, warning them that their security was in danger because there might be fighting. That item was passed on and arrived at the headquarters in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say, "On the night in which the fighting broke out ..." Please be as precise as you can and as your memory allows. Are you talking about the night before? Is this the night of the 8th of May or the night after fighting started on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the early hours of the day in which fighting broke out. I seem to remember it was the 8th of May. I would have to refer to the logbook, but I do believe it was the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall more specifically about what the information was and what the directions or -- strike that. What the information received from the HVO was? Was this a suggestion that SpaBat might want to follow or was SpaBat ordered out of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a suggestion, if I might add almost an order, because our security was endangered when we heard or when we -- it was suggested to us that we had better leave, I suppose they were discharging themselves of any responsibility should any harm ensue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did the Spanish Battalion or the element that was in Mostar at that time do in response to this information, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aside from passing on this information to the higher echelons in UNPROFOR, it was made clear that our task was what it was. The chief of SpaBat decided to withdraw from the area and to move more towards the west of Mostar some one to one and a half kilometres away from the conflict area, and the patrol was then stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges now, because it may come up in the next few minutes in reference to various things, from the position, the new position that the Spanish Battalion element took up you say to the west of Mostar, did they continue to have a view on the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We had a view of the city not in detail. Perhaps we missed out, or they missed out at checkpoints or crossroads, but yes, a general view of the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please allow me to say something at this stage. You've just said that after having received the information from the HVO of an imminent threat of an attack, the person in charge of the battalion who was touring Mostar decided to leave the area, and that unit had been given a mission, and did they have to patrol the area? Was that part of the assignment of these men? And in the event of an imminent danger, were these men entitled to leave or did the head of the battalion contact his superior to -- so that the latter would give him an order telling him that he could leave the place? Could you please tell us more about this. Because when you're in the army, you have very -- a very specific assignment, and if you change your assignment, this means that you've received an order. So could you shed some light on this for me, please, and tell me how these men who were patrolling around town left the place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The mission was to be present in the city. They could not use force nor undertake any other mission. They had to be there so that the civilian population be aware that the UN was there in the city. The moment conflict broke out, the moment that the Spanish troops' security was in danger, the chief of the battalion decided to withdraw the troops from the conflict area because its mission was not to keep peace. The Spanish Battalion took on this mission of being present aside from the EU and other missions. But the moment the security of the troops was in danger, the order to withdraw was given but to remain around the area in order to be able to inform UNPROFOR, but not to participate in anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the witness next to be shown Exhibit P 01717, the logbook. And I believe in the English version it will be on page 58. In the Spanish version, I can only refer to the -- what we refer to as the ERN on the page, which I believe it will be at ERN 0167814, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness BJ, as soon as you have that on your screen, if you'd just let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is -- while we're doing this, I'm just wondering out loud - and no disrespect to the Spanish language - I wonder if, for the witness's purposes, whether it would be easier to provide him with the hard copy of the Spanish version since he presumably is the one making most frequent reference to the Spanish version, and then we can use the English on -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All right. That's exactly what I would have done had I been in your shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that we can save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Because I know from the witness he can turn to the particular entries by date I think quite quickly himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So if you can find your entry, sir, for the 9th of May, or the diary entry for the 9th of May, that would be very helpful, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can find this -- these references, and I'll ask you -- then I'll ask you several questions and of course the Judges may have questions. In your report on that day, it says: "At 0500 hours in the Mostar area, the HVO carried out an attack using artillery, mortars, and heavy and small arms on the Muslim quarter in the city. The attack centred on the American bridge (Tito's bridge) and the armija headquarters. Due to the fighting the company that was deployed in the city had to retreat south-west of the city." Now, let's stop there for a moment. In reference to the questions that were raised a moment ago, the reference to the company retreating south-west of the city, is that consistent with the information that had been received from the HVO and that what you've told the Judges is that this unit then did withdraw to an area west or south-west of the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I have been saying before. When we received the news item, the company withdrew to the hospital area to the south-west of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going on in that entry: "The access routes to the city were blocked. The fighting continued throughout the day. The HVO controls all access routes to the city. Citizens were observed gathering in the football stadium and being moved out of the city in buses. At the checkpoints on all roads the HVO was making the passage of our units difficult with trivial excuses (asking to see the documents, et cetera)." To the best of your knowledge, sir, is that an accurate entry in terms of what you knew and heard and understood to be happening on the 9th of May in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, completely. Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct for us to understand, and most importantly for the Judges to understand, that when it says, for example, civilians were observed gathering in the football stadium, these were observations that were being made from the SpaBat element that had taken some ground just outside of town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is news coming from the units deployed in Mostar. I don't know whether the news arrived when they were moving towards the west or south-west, but in any case, the news was coming from the units deployed in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Still directing your attention to the -- to the 9th of May, but not reflected, I don't believe, in this particular entry, can you tell the Judges whether there was any incident or situation that day in which the BiH army officer Pasalic was held or delayed somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because I was there. General Pasalic was escorted from Jablanica for a meeting held with General Petkovic, if I'm not mistaken, and at the entrance to Mostar he was stopped at a Croat checkpoint, and he was not allowed to go through. HVO knew about the movement of the general, because when commanding officers moved about we had to inform about these movements, and with a profusion of apologies he was detained some four to five hours, I can't remember. Because I was involved in telephone negotiations with Mr. Vasic [as interpreted]. And at the end of those very many hours, and because we were responsible for his security, we obtained from Mr. Vasic the authority for Mr. Pasalic to come to our detachment headquarters, and for the sake of his security we took the general to the Medjugorje headquarters, and he was there for two to three days. That's when the attack on Mostar took place, the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript you say that you -- in English we read Mr. Vasic, but in the translation I heard Kosic. Who was the person with whom you negotiated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bozic. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bozic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was deputy minister of defence, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The full name of this individual, if you recall, sir, was that Slobodan Bozic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. He was the person with whom we got in touch when we had any problems or when we had to negotiate with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he speak Spanish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, English. And we had an interpreter -- well, I had a Croat-Spanish interpreter in order to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this individual, sir, Mr. Bozic, you say he was the deputy minister of defence. He was the immediate deputy to Defence Minister Bruno Stojic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so. I think he was the second in command, yes, from the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just looking ahead for the moment, did you have a number of dealings with Mr. Bozic during your tour in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Every time there was to be negotiations over a convoy which had been detained on its way to Jablanica, or when communications were cut, we almost always talked to Mr. Bozic, either me personally or any other officer in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm looking further, and I'm sorry I didn't direct your attention to it before, but also on the 9th of May in the operational journal there is indeed, I believe, further down the page, a reference to the fact that Mr. Pasalic was being delayed for -- it says "waiting for more than seven hours, and then they all moved to Kresevo where they spent the night." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, seven hours. Yes, you're right. Seven hours. I said four to five earlier. Well, it was seven then. I can't quite remember. I suppose it must be seven since this was so written in the logbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you understand, sir, again just as you knew Mr. Bozic, did you understand that Mr. Pasalic was the overall commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the area of Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. Yes, we were clear that that was so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, in your experience as a professional military man and as a senior officer yourself, would the HVO have had any reason to keep Mr. Pasalic out of Mostar for those approximately seven hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that clearly calls for speculation and once again we get into the area of the Prosecution turning a witness into an expert without giving us the proper notice and opportunity to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me restate the question. As to being an expert, Your Honour, this man is a professional soldier. All his career, having graduated from the academy in 1976, I believe. I believe he can -- he can express a view on certain military matters without being designated as a testifying expert as such. As to -- I think he can tell us generally in his experience why would -- why would some opposing force want to detain the commanding officer of the other side, what the advantages of that would be at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, firstly I'm not disputing the witness's experience and ability as a military officer. That's not the question. The question is that there are rules to be followed if the Prosecution wishes to designate him as an expert. Secondly, Your Honour, the question that he's being asked is speculative. The issue is not whether he can imagine any reasons for what the HVO may have done or may not have done, he's being asked to speculate as to what the motivations of persons within the HVO may have been, and we don't even know who these persons are that he's being asked to speculate about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask some additional questions, Your Honour. I'll rephrase the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's just the way the question is formulated, because you can achieve the same result without the Defence standing to its feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness BJ, during this time, were you conducting most of the negotiations with the HVO side to obtain the freedom of movement of Mr. Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I negotiated with Mr. Bozic the freedom of movement for General Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that was my next question. Throughout these conversations over this, at least here 7-hour period, did you have -- were all your conversations or dealings with Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Not all seven hours. We kept on phoning up. When communication went down, we kept on phoning each other on and off. We were not on the phone for seven hours in a row. We were on and off two or three hours but this in the period of seven hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And perhaps you can just tell the Judges if you recall, how long was it before Mr. Pasalic was able to go on about his business and move about freely after being detained or delayed in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How long did it take for him to regain freedom of movement? Well, if there was seven hours' delay, once the permit or authorisation was given for us to take him to our headquarters, he was allowed to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then how long was he at your headquarters before he then was free to move about the area without Spanish Battalion escort, if at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 48 to 72 hours before he was returned to his area in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, when you spent a lot of time over the telephone to make sure that Mr. Pasalic can move around freely, what motivated you? What did you do this? What was the reason behind all of this? Why did you want Mr. Pasalic to be able to move around freely? Was it because of the consequences that could have? Why did you actually do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as pursuant to the agreements between the parties, UNPROFOR could move freely in the area, and if escorts were undertaken, they were undertaken for VIPs known to both parties that should be able to move freely, and the security was the responsibility of SpaBat. Some eight or nine months before, an armoured vehicle, I believe a French vehicle, had killed a Serb, I believe, I can't remember, and we were afraid that something might happen to General Pasalic. It was our mission, therefore, to escort him and to take him to a safe place and to keep him in a safe place. That was our concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So insofar as Mr. Pasalic was a prominent figure, you as part of your assignment were to escort him when he moved about, and in this particular case he couldn't, and this is why you contacted Mr. Bozic. Is this how we are to understand what you did at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We had held a meeting at Jablanica. Mr. Pasalic was there, and we had agreed with the armija and the HVO that they would meet in Jablanica with representatives from both parties. And on the way back from Jablanica to Mostar was when General Pasalic was stopped at a checkpoint, he was threatened. His escort called me and told me that there were threats, that the vehicle might be assaulted, that there was some danger to General Pasalic's security.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps it will assist us on the topic, I've jumped over a document or two and come back. If I could have the witness direct his attention to Exhibit P 02273, which is a sitrep, which is sitrep 168, apparently for the 10th of May, 1993. It should be found -- the entry should be found, I believe, on pages 3 or 4 -- and 4 of the English version and page 1 to 2 of the Spanish version. Let me make sure I've given you the right ... Sorry, Your Honour. I'm not -- ah, okay. Yes. The top of page 4 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you can find the reference, sir, in that document, it says -- some might call them bullet items, and at one point it says: "General Pasalic, commander of the 4th Corps of the BH army, is in Spanish detachment in Drecevo and some HVO checkpoints have been put up around the detachment in order to prevent him from leaving." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it. It's here in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And following on that, it says: "The deputy commander of the Capljina brigade showed up in the detachment, demanding that General Pasalic be handed over, which the detachment commander refused." Were you being briefed and kept advised of these developments as they were ongoing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed continuously when the second in command was demanding that the general be surrendered to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And your testimony is that as a result of all of these events it was approximately somewhere, 48 to 72 hours before Mr. Pasalic could actually then go on about his way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I do not recall the period of time. I would have to look into this, but I think that that was between 48 and 72 hours that he was actually there within the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If we could go then next to Exhibit P 02241. Yes.
