utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Before we go on to the next exhibit, sir, could you take a look at the next page of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please scroll up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And you have point 3 "Operaciones Mostar." Now, paragraph 3, in Spanish, it says: "Se han observado concentracion de civiles en el campo de futbol ..." And so this refers to the concentration of civilians on the football stadium. Now, did you send men to go and see what was going on? Because apparently there was a football match. So did you send anybody to see what was going on? They were not attending a football match.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once we were in the western part of the city, in the area of the hospitals, there was no possibility of movement, so we knew that there was a conflict within the area of the hospital. And we could see the football field and we could see the movements, and the company was there and did inform to us that there were some -- some -- there was something happening there, and not because there was a match going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With binoculars you weren't able to see the football field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the hospital, yes, you could see the football field and all the movements that was -- that were taking place. But there was a shorter distance from the hospital to the football field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Following up on the President's questions, if we could now go to Exhibit P 02241, which is an intrep 167 for the 9th of May, 1993. I believe the information will be at page 4 of the English version and page 2 of the Spanish version. Sir -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you find on -- forgive me. I think my own note is wrong, so let me just reorient myself. At the bottom of page 3 of the English version, but if you see -- your section number 1.2 areas and then you'll see Mostar, and then the entry "Shelling," then it says: "At 0500 hours mortar attacks were launched against the Muslim sector from HVO positions." Now, I think other -- I will not need to read out loud everything that follows, but in reference to the question that His Honour Judge Antonetti raised a moment ago, if you read on down in that section, it says: "Other information. The Spanish section on duty in the city made its way to the outskirts of Mostar but its way to the 'illegible' was barred by HVO personnel. At 1246 hours buses driven by armed HVO personnel and loaded with people were seen arriving at the football ground at --" again illegible. I don't know if you can help us with some of these. Maybe the Spanish is clearer to you. "At 1313 hours the arrival of more civilians was observed (this time standing up) in buses driven by armed personnel." Now, referring to the question by Judge Antonetti, did you understand that the Spanish Battalion element that was still in the immediate vicinity of the Mostar had such a position and such observation equipment, binoculars or what have you, they were able to make these observations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. The company had not withdrawn from the city, it had withdrawn itself from the city centre but was in an area next to the football field and could observe the movement of people with a number of observation measures, normal, standard observation measures, be it binoculars and other devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Further down on that same page before we leave the document, moving away from Mostar for a moment, on the same page you see an entry -- or at least in the English version it's the same page. Forgive me, it may or may not be in the Spanish. The section for Jablanica. Page 3, I believe, of the Spanish version. And under that section it talks about act -- excuse me. "At 1247 came confirmation of HVO attack against the Muslim battalion at presume Gornji Dreznica. The attacks were launched at 13 --" Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I do see that completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So in addition to what was happening in Mostar at this time, were you continuing to receive reports from the Spanish Battalion element in the Jablanica area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also we received information from a detachment in Jablanica and they were telling us what was happening there and what they could observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in connection with the observations that we've been talking about, can you tell the Judges was some video footage made by the Spanish army, by components of the Spanish Battalion on the 9th of May, showing some of the things that we have talked about so far today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a video footage but I cannot recall whether it was in relation to the 9th of May or the exact dates. I cannot recall that. But, yes, there was video footage that was taken of the movement of civilians on the part of the armed HVO forces, transferring the civilians from one area to another. I cannot recall the -- the date, and I did not see the video footage. It was sent as a document to Spain. Yes, I did see it, but I cannot recall the date. I cannot remember whether it was the 9th or the 11th or the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me break that down into a couple of smaller pieces. You confirm that a video was made around this time; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you personally see the video yourself, and did you see the content of the video played before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw the video in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did the video show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The movement of civilian personnel, men, women and children, being led by armed forces of the Croat army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was this video sent to Spanish army headquarters in Madrid, or at least in Spain if not Madrid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. It was sent to the headquarters as part of the information that had been received, and I am certain that it was also published on the Spanish TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, did you ever receive any complaints from the HVO that this video had been made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand in relation to the copy. Yes, we had received complaints that we had made this video, because it was not part of the intelligence, but, yes, we had indeed make or produced a video and published it, broadcast it. I did not receive the complaint, but the head of the Canarias group actually received the complaint himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges as best you recall what the complaint was and who made the complaint.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall who actually made the complaint. I think I believe that it could be Bozic, but I do not recall. But basically it was to do with the complaint that it was a lack of loyalty to them because we had broadcast or we had produced images which could have led people to believe that there were facts that were not real.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall there being some reference, as you just said -- I'm just looking at the transcript, at least the translation, that it was put to you that this was somehow showing a lack of loyalty to the Croats or to the HVO? In what sense was any loyalty owed to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Just so we're clear about this. The question is whether the witness would like to speculate about whether a person he thinks may have been Mr. Bozic may have said to a person in charge of the -- his unit, which this witness did not see or hear at all. Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The question is the question I put to the witness, and which he just said in page 67, line 2, "... basically it was to do with the complaint that it was a lack of loyalty to them because we had broadcast or we had produced images ..." I'm simply asking the witness if he recalls more about that and specifically anything in reference to the issue of "loyalty."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could you answer the question, because apparently we see there was some complaint, complaints made because of the fact that this video was broadcast on Spanish television.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was. There was an official complaint on the part of the HVO to our group for having broadcast images, in fact images which had been recorded. I do not recall precisely the reason. I could not affirm this, but I do believe that the reasons alluded to was because of the lack of loyalty and because we had not informed them prior to the broadcasting of these images, and I believe that that's where it was left at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask, Witness, were you involved when this was discussed? Were you a party to the discussions about how to react to this complaint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not personally involved when the complaint was received by the colonel, but I knew that he was in the office that was next door, and the group, the leader of the group, the head of the group actually told us what had taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, are you going to show the video or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure whether I should raise this in front of the witness or not. There is an issue about that, but I'm just not sure how to proceed. I can -- let me see if I can -- I don't know if the witness can help us on this but I'll ask questions and see if we can achieve it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness BJ, can you tell us whether to your knowledge that video still exists? Is it still in the custody of the Spanish army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The video was sent to our headquarters in Madrid, and I believe that it must be archived somewhere. That is my opinion. I don't know. I have not seen it again. I don't know if it has been lost or gone astray or stored, but I do know that it was broadcast on Spanish television. Perhaps the Spanish TV stations could have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, just to make the record as complete as possible, did you have any involvement in any efforts in the past several years to locate the videotape at the Spanish army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I did not have any responsibility of that matter when I was in Spain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time all I can tell -- all I can do, really, is inform the Chamber that the Office of the Prosecutor has made a repeated request for that tape to be produced to us for a number of years and has never -- the tape has never been produced. It has been represented to us that the tape cannot be located. That's all I can say further at this moment. There is another -- I can indicate to the Court that there's a future -- there's another Spanish Battalion witness who confirms the fact that a video was made that I believe will give evidence in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Spain there are a number of television channels, but there's the TVE, the major television channel. Now, to the best of your recollections, was that video -- what television channel was the video shown on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Affirmative. What I know and what I recall, I cannot say it on a hundred per cent, but it was seen -- it was actually broadcast on the TVE, the Spanish network.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] TVE that broadcast it. But you're not quite sure. You're not a hundred per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not on a hundred per cent certainty because I wasn't there, so I don't know what was actually broadcast on the Spanish TV station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please resume, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward, sir, but still early in this 9th, 10th of May time period. Can you tell us, sir, around this time was a Spanish officer by the name of Lieutenant -- I think in this particular instance probably, unfortunately, the name doesn't matter, but Lieutenant Castellanos was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 11th of May we went to the east of Mostar to take some blood products, and during the time that we were there, we went through the eastern Muslim area, and we were the subject of a mortar which was launched, and as a direct result Lieutenant Castellanos was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's take that a bit further. Do you recall how it was that the request had been made or how it was that the Spanish Battalion had been -- become involved in moving some medical products or blood into the East Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, demarches were made with the Croat authorities for blood plasma to be taken to the eastern part of Mostar to the hospital in the Muslim area, and we even reached an agreement of cease-fire of about one hour, if I recall correctly, at around 12.00 noon, and around 2.00 p.m., two armoured vehicles of Spain went to the Muslim area and we delivered the blood plasma in the Muslim hospital. And the agreement was that we had to actually move a Catholic priest from this area. I cannot recall his name. And we went in search for this Catholic priest at his domicile in the Muslim area, and when we did this we were the subject of a number of mortars which had been launched, and as a result Lieutenant Castellanos was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Were you present when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I understood you correctly, would it be fair to say that there was -- an agreement had been reached, the quid pro quo, if you would, was that some blood would be allowed to go into East Mostar and on the other hand you would bring -- the Spanish Battalion would bring a Catholic priest out of the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, as much as you recall of the approximate location. I don't -- strike that. Not the location in terms of a street name, but what was the area? What was the nature of the area where Lieutenant Castellanos was hit? Was he in an open area? Was it a visible area, or what more can you tell us about the nature of the location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Muslim area where Lieutenant Castellanos was killed, we went in search of the Catholic priest in an open area of courtyards. And when I went back three or four days later with the UN police to undertake the investigation into the death of Lieutenant Castellanos, we looked at the area where the explosions had fallen and where the shots had been fired from and where the mortars had actually fallen, and we looked at the area where Lieutenant Castellanos had actually been killed, and it was an open, visible area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the time that Lieutenant Castellanos was killed, was he wearing a -- a blue helmet identifying him as a UN member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all with blue helmets. We were all bearing or wearing blue helmets. As well as the blue helmets, there was an interpreter who also happened to be carrying a blue helmet, and a Muslim officer, he was also accompanying us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, approximately how many mortar rounds were fired before the round that struck and killed Lieutenant Castellanos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area was an area of a lot of explosions in the area. Not only in the area where we were but particularly where we were two -- two shells had actually been launched, and not only in front of us but also behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. My question to you is, if I can ask you, please, not the overall explosions in a broader area but in the immediate area where you and this Spanish Battalion component was at the time, was it these -- specifically these two mortar shells, only two mortar shots were fired, one of which killed the lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I understand that not two. Two shells were launched practically simultaneously, one in front, one behind, and I think it was the two shells. I cannot really tell you which one of those two shells actually killed the lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You said, sir, that from the location you could see where the positions of the mortar were. Can you tell us where these positions were from where the shots had been fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Mount Hum [Realtime transcript read in error "Hul"]. From Mount Hum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again following that line of thinking, you said shots, but on the basis of your knowledge as a militaryman, your technical knowledge, was that a mortar shell? Where did the shell come from and what was the calibre the shell that fell? Can you give us some more specific technical details about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were explosions of two grenades of mortars of 82 millimetres -- of a mortar of 82 millimetres. It was two grenades. That was as a result of the investigation and the [indiscernible] must be there somewhere. Also as a result of the UNPROFOR police investigation that was there with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this type of weaponry and ammunition, and do you use -- do you have a viewfinder, and do you have charts for firing or do you not use this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's -- it's in relation to particular obstacles. It has a trajectory that follows a curve, and this is done usually behind a certain obstacle in relation to certain buildings or a house. I don't know if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I don't know -- yes, that does answer my question, but I'm not quite sure. I don't know whether the person who is opening fire has to calculate where his target is, or can you open fire without doing that? These 82-millimetre mortars. And you were there -- is that -- did it just happen randomly or did it happen because you calculated the firing on the basis of the charts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I to understand the question if they had been seen before they had been launched or when they had been launched against us, I cannot affirm that tacitly. I was convinced, because I was there, and I do believe that first the group went there in search of the Catholic priest, and there was another escort group, and perhaps in relation to the distance or in relation to the time that the grenade takes from being launched to arrival, maybe the grenades fell on the same site where we had been previously located and maybe they hit the lieutenant, but I cannot affirm that we were in their direct view and therefore we were the object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me follow up again to the Judges' questions which is part of what was trying to come to earlier. You've told us in the last few minutes your group was moving around the area for some time, trying to find this Catholic priest, if I understand correctly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not really a whole lot of time. We knew exactly where we were going to. The Muslim -- the Muslim official was leading us, and it was about 500 metres to 1.000 metres between the armoured vehicles, and where the Catholic priest was, the armoured vehicles couldn't go through that because they were twisting and they're narrow streets. And so we came under small-arms fire, so we had to be extremely careful. We had to go -- proceed street-by-street, taking care of our safety, and so this took a great deal of time. This is why we have to move through courtyards, et cetera, before we actually came to the Catholic priest. It would have taken about 15 minutes in all actually rescuing the priest, picking him up and taking him out of there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. So you exited the armoured personnel carrier, you're moving about on foot for approximately a 15-minute period, and you also came under small-arms fire; is that correct? No translation, sorry. Sir, to repeat my question: So you were moving around on foot for approximately 15 minutes and you also indicated that you came -- your group came under small-arms fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apparently we have a technical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, could you repeat your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were -- your group -- this group that you were moving about with after looking for the Catholic priest, you said you were on foot, moving about the area for approximately 15 minutes. At some point your group came under small-arms fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. Affirmative. But I'm not saying that small arms were actually directed at us. It was taking place while we were looking for the priest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. And my next question then was: The two mortar rounds, were those the only two mortar rounds that were fired at that time or were there other mortar rounds that had impacted in your immediate vicinity? I mean immediately around you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were other shells. There were other mortar rounds. We were going through very narrow streets, and we were hearing all of these explosions. I didn't actually feel that they were close to us, but I could hear them around us. It's not like these two ones, one of the ones that killed the lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can have the witness be shown, right before the break - I believe we can finish this - Exhibit P 09612. We can give a hard copy if it's going to be -- maybe it's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just so the record is clear, if you can look at the photograph that's on you, when you said earlier -- it came out in the translation -- at least, on transcript, as Mount Hul. Were you referring to Mount Hum, and is that the feature in the photograph that you understood the mortar round came from, the position from which the mortar round came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. Yes. That's exactly the place where I think that the mortar shells came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There seems to be a certain discrepancy. The document you have indicated shows the Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe I got the number wrong, Your Honour. My apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It is 14. 14, not 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For the record, Exhibit P 09614. But this is the photo -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm getting different information here myself. According -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, and perhaps we can sort it out during the break, if necessary. Ms. Winner is telling me that it is in fact 612. The bundle may be -- unfortunately, your bundle may be in error for whatever reason. I have the same -- I have the same thing, Your Honour. My 9612 is the Vranica building. You're right. So they must have been ... For the purpose -- perhaps for completing this particular part of your testimony before the break, because I think we're about due for a break, Your Honour, if I'm not mistaken, the feature that is shown -- do you have the photograph now of a hill, of a -- overlooking the town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recognise that feature -- whatever the number of this document is, do you recognise that feature as Mount Hum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's exactly right. Yes. There's no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there must be an error in the numbering that we'll have to sort out. Sorry. And, Your Honour, I suggest that may be the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Before we take the break, we have the photograph in front of us and we see the hill. Sir, you're telling us that the shot came from the hill. Who was on the hill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were positions occupied by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right at the top of the hill, in the middle of the hill, or to the bottom of the hill? Because we can see the whole hill on the photograph. You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to our information, the mortars were behind the hill. You see -- you see that cross on the right? It's right behind that cross where you have the mortars. And probably even to this day you will find those mortars right there behind that cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you take up the pointer and show us on the photograph. Point to where the mortars were. Is that possible, Madam Usher? We have the most sophisticated and up-to-date technology here, but maybe we can take a pencil or something and indicate that on the photograph itself where the mortars were, to the best of your recollection and knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in -- it's behind what I'm pointing at. It's actually behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Behind. And it was coming from that way, making a trajectory, a parabolic trajectory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Affirmative. You see, a mortar always follows a very curved line. So on top of a hill probably you had the observers who were directing the mortar people when to fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So for technical reasons we're going to have to take a break now, take the technical break. It's 25 minutes to 1, and we'll reconvene at 5 minutes to 1, which will give us 50 more minutes. I hope you'll get through in that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we have a photograph here, and are you going to be tendering this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If we can have the marked photograph given an IC number, please, by the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is a marked document, IC 00025. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just before moving on, Your Honour, my understanding is that in terms of what's in e-court and what's in the official record, the numbers, the exhibit numbers and the item matches. It was apparently when the bundles were put together, the hard copy bundles, which are not the official set, there were some errors made, unfortunately. My understanding is that in the actual e-court record the numbering is correct. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, we've come up to the point where Mr. -- or excuse me, Lieutenant Castellanos was hit by the mortar round and then some additional investigation or information that was obtained about that. Was there an effort to get medical care for Lieutenant Castellanos immediately and to get an ambulance into the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. First we -- he was treated at the Muslim hospital in the West Mostar area, and once there, then we called an ambulance, a Spanish ambulance which was stationed in the west of the city. There were some problems for the ambulance to be let through the checkpoints, the Croat checkpoints, that is. The General Praljak was, as it happened, nearby. He was asked to give authority for the ambulance to get through so that the lieutenant could be picked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And so the record is clear, and I'm not sure it's even in the transcript at this point, the individual that you just identified when you said the general, were you talking about a man named Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Then General Praljak -- Mr. Praljak then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you -- had you known Mr. Praljak prior to this occasion on the 11th of May, 1993, or had any dealings with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had visited or, rather, he had visited the Spanish detachment, and I believe that the day before blood was transported to Mostar the negotiations were undertaken with him. I believe he was the one who in fact did request a cease-fire so that the blood could be transported to the Muslim area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where were these negotiations -- excuse me. Where did these negotiations take place? That is, you say, the day before, that Mr. Praljak was involved in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm not -- if I'm not wrong, on the afternoon on the 10th. It was on the afternoon of the 10th, on the afternoon of the 10th at the Medjugorje detachment. I'm not a hundred per cent certain, but I think that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it a face-to-face meeting with Mr. Praljak or was this done over the telephone or can you give us any additional information, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a face-to-face negotiation. I did not participate directly. I was present, but it was S5 normally in charge of such negotiations. I was present in order to know which escorts were needed for a given action or movement. So it was a face-to-face negotiation. He came to the Spanish detachment, as I seem to recall. I mean, he came quite a few times, so I don't know whether at that time he was there for that particular negotiation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you said that after Lieutenant Castellanos was hit, that you were trying to obtain this medical care and get an ambulance into the area, and somehow Mr. Praljak came -- became involved. Can you tell us a little bit more about, if you know, how it was that Mr. Praljak was in the area or how he came to be in communication with your unit about this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we went to look for our ambulance, our ambulance which was outside Mostar, our units had withdrawn following the attack, but they stayed on the sidelines when attacks took place. So we went to look for that ambulance to pick up our injured lieutenant. When we tried to return through the western zone in order to arrive at the Tito bridge to pick up our lieutenant, when we tried to get back, the Croat checkpoints did not allow the ambulance to go through, and so we were involved in this discussion as to whether we were let through or not. And quite by chance - I mean by chance - the vehicle of Mr. Praljak came by, and given that my accompanying person knew him, he approached him, explained what had happened, explained that there was an injured officer on the other side, and requested that the ambulance be let through, and admittedly automatically Mr. Praljak said the ambulance ought to be let through, and it was thus done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, how Mr. Praljak was dressed was at the time that you saw him on the 11th of May in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see him. It was not me. It was not I who approached him to ask him to let the ambulance through. It was a colleague of mine, another major, if I'm not wrong. I'd seen Mr. Praljak the day before, and he was always in his uniform, so I suppose he was in his uniform that day, but I cannot, obviously, say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say -- sorry. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I note a certain contradiction, because I thought that you had said that you addressed General Praljak because you had known him and met him before when he came. Now you say that you were not there. So could you perhaps clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was there when the negotiations took place the day before but not when we negotiated for the ambulance to come into Mostar. I had stayed at the hospital with the injured lieutenant, and it was my colleague who went in an armoured vehicle to call in the ambulance from where it was, and this colleague -- this colleague of mine was the one who met with Mr. Praljak, who informed him of the fact that we had an injured officer. So it wasn't on that day that I saw him. It was the day before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And I suppose that your companero also knew Praljak and had seen him before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was the head of S5, so he knew him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, on the day before then, when you said -- now clarified that you did see him and meet with Mr. Praljak at the SpaBat location in Medjugorje, and you said he was dressed in a uniform. Did you notice at that time what insignia or patches he wore indicating of what military force or armed force he was a part of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember the insignia or badge, but through information we had about General Praljak and from what we knew, we knew that at some stage he had the HVO insignia, but I cannot say that he was wearing that insignia on that particular day. I cannot recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What information -- was Mr. Praljak -- just follow on your answer just now. Was Mr. Praljak such a person that he was someone that the previous component of the Spanish army that had been there before the Canarias group, that he was the type of person that they would have compiled information about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't quite follow your question. Mr. Praljak, I think, was just beginning. He did not have authority in the HVO army, but he did have a certain authority, and it was -- he was beginning to be an interesting person to know and to have contacts with, but I cannot really remember if then he was the chief of anything. I think that's when he was beginning to be known in our area. I don't know whether this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me follow up by saying did you -- let me come back. I've just been handed a note. I don't know if the translation is correct or not on the page -- earlier when I asked you about what military force that he had been a part of, did you say HVO or did you say HV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, HV it says here, but I said that we knew that he was wearing the HV insignia, the Croat army insignia. Later, I saw the HVO insignia on his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in talking to your colleague, the one who apparently had the direct discussion with Mr. Praljak that day about obtaining movement for the ambulance, did your colleague report to you anything more about how it was that Mr. Praljak had obtained a quick resolution of that matter? Did he say if he issued an order? Did he go somewhere else and meet with someone? If you know, did your colleague provide you any more information about how it was that Mr. Praljak was able to obtain the movement for the ambulance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite simply he issued an order to the checkpoint and admittedly automatically the ambulance was let through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one point of clarification, please. During this period and when the ambulance had to go through, as far as you know what was the highest military authority in the Mostar area on the HVO side? Who --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that the head, of the army of the HVO army was General Petkovic, if I'm not wrong. And he -- and General Praljak was beginning to gain a certain authority. But right now who the head, the number one of the HVO was in Mostar I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can move forward, then, apology to the usher for putting that document back. If I could direct the witness's attention to Exhibit P 01717, the logbook. And for the courtroom, page 72. Page 72 of the English version. And if you can find your entry, sir, for the 26th of May, 1993. The first item on that day, if you have it, it says: "Isolated rifle shots could be heard in Mostar during the day. An attempt was made today to get a humanitarian aid convoy into the Muslim quarter in the city. The passage through a checkpoint was barred by the HVO. They insisted on checking the cargo first and then, once they had done that, to discuss who would receive the cargo." Can you just tell the Judges, what was the -- in reference to this and around the end of May, 1993, what was the situation with being able to get humanitarian aid into the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, obviously the days, you know, I cannot recall exactly when humanitarian aid was allowed through and when not. You can see what we attempted to do. On that day we tried to make a humanitarian convoy arrive, but it was impossible because the Croat checkpoint prevented this -- prevented this convoy from going through. We had to negotiate day by day and case by case the humanitarian aid convoys. And this is why not very many humanitarian aid convoys arrived at the city. I cannot say -- I cannot recall whether this happened every day or every week. I would have to go through all the documents in order to ascertain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you to go to the page 75 -- well, to 30th of May in your log. And on the English, page 75. I would like to ask you a question about this entry. It says: "Civilians continued to cross by bus from one bank of the river Neretva to the other in Mostar. The HVO selected the Muslims who were then -- who then were able to cross, and the SpaBat responded to this situation by sending a letter of protest." Do you recall any particular criteria or did the Spanish Battalion come to know what criteria were being -- was being applied by the HVO to decide which Muslims could cross and which ones could not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honour, if I could object. It does seem that that's asking the witness to speculate. Can we please establish whether that was based on his own knowledge or on information, and, if so, from whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask an additional series of questions, Your Honour, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in your entry you said that as a result this of situation SpaBat responded by sending a letter of protest. Do you know whether SpaBat received any information about the basis for which these -- in response to the protest or otherwise, the basis on which these decisions were being made as to which Muslims could cross and which ones could not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember. But I don't believe there was an answer to this letter. Perhaps there was an oral answer but not a written letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Down below, in the next entry, about halfway through, it says: "When the buses reached the HVO zone, they let the Croats pass but not Muslims." Did that situation come to your attention and was anything more said about that? Was that the subject of a Spanish Battalion protest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were familiar with the situation. The mixed commission wanted everyone to go back to their place, whether west or east. So those people who had been left in the west because of the change in ethnic group, so to speak, should go back to their own place. But in our attempt to get people to move freely, HVO prevented Muslims from passing or going to the western side of the city. I remember that a written protest was lodged on the 27th or 28th, but I don't know whether there were further written protests or whether this was raised with the mixed commission or committee when we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go to or be shown Exhibit P 02583. That will be, I believe, on page 8 of the English version and page 3 of the Spanish document. Just one -- one quick question, if you can assist us. The -- there's an entry on that page saying that there were continued problems with the line that was supposed to have facilitated the movement of persons from one side of the river to the other. Under "Other information." Can you tell us just what was the line? Maybe it was the problem of the English translation, but "continued problems with the line." Do you know what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When there's talk about the line, we're talking about the confrontation lines or the separation lines, the Bulevar and the river areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But this seems to be making reference to the line that was supposed to have facilitated the movement of persons, which doesn't seem to quite fit with that. If you don't know, you can simply -- certainly tell us that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, reading the document, it's as though a comma were missing. "Line --" "problems are continuing along the line, that should facilitate movement from one side to the other." At least this is how I understand it when I read the Spanish draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could next direct your attention, with the registry's assistance, to P 04698. And in particular, if you will, please -- well, looking at that document, if you can, you have a chance to see, so you can tell us overall what the document is. Let's start with that. And tell us, please, if you need to see other parts of the document to answer my question. Is this a -- what type of document is this that we're looking at now? Is this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I -- could I see the whole of the document and see the first page of the document, because I can't see the first page. Actually, it may be a report -- do we have the other page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm being told this is apparently the first page. Okay. I'm -- apparently not, so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the second page, then? The next page. It looks like an insum referring to Mostar. It might be part of an intrep if it was issued by S2, as it says -- as it says on the upper corner, right, that might well be so, but I can't quite see. But certainly it is a document issued by the Canarias group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question to you was about just in terms of the form of the document in case it might come up with other similar documents. This looks different than the ones we've been looking at primarily today. It doesn't look like the daily report. Is this something else? And, if so, how would you describe this type of document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it might be part of an insum, which is a specific document issued at a given time for a given reason about a specific question. It could be part of an intrep because the situation required that the document be expanded, given the seriousness of the situation, and it could also be part of the report drafted once the group, the Canarias group, finished its mission and had to report on the whole duration of the mission. I cannot quite say that now. But it is an intelligence document no doubt. S2 intelligence, that without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I understand correctly, the witness is confirming that this is evidently part of a document. I think either we admit a whole document from first to last page, or we don't admit it at all, especially if it's not certain what part of the document is being admitted. [In English] I was just warned by my assistant that we cannot see the date on the document. So that is in addition to what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I don't believe I can assist the Chamber any further on my feet at this moment. I can certainly make additional inquiries. Let me just -- give me a moment to speak with some of my colleagues and see if they can help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I can't -- unfortunately, Your Honour, I can't assist the Chamber any more at the moment, but the witness is -- I can say that obviously the witness said he does recognise the document as a SpaBat report, but whether there's other pages to the document we'll have to do a further investigation, I'm afraid. Sir, if you can look at the type of report. Was it customary that at the end of a mission the group would make a report, some sort of after-mission, if you will, post-mission report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Once the mission is over, the group that withdraws from the area draws up a full report on its six-month tour and draws up a report. Each body involved, each body of officers involved and troops involved have to draw up a report for what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may make a contribution here. At the bottom of the document in Spanish we can see "AGT Canarias pagina number 33." So this document is an excerpt or is -- comes after another document, because we have page numbers which don't coincide here. As we know that in the Spanish documents of the Spanish Bat there are a great number of stamps, these stamps on page 33 are not entrance or exit stamps. These are just stamps to prove that the documents have been handed over to the Tribunal. So I assume that this stems from a more general document. The Prosecution will make the necessary investigation. That's your job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, and as I say, I can't assist the Chamber any further at this particular moment, although I do see that one of the stamps on the page indicates that authorisation to produce one copy of document number consisting of pages 33 to 45. So that -- it may very well be that for whatever reason those were the particular specific pages produced to the Tribunal, but we will make further inquiries, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only question I would like to raise as far as this document is concerned, I'd like to know whether this document comes from the Spanish Battalion or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No doubt at all about that. It is a Spanish Battalion document drawn by Section 2 of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, on that -- on that note, and it may be more difficult in the electronic format, but if you could be -- if the registry could assist by allowing you to page through several of these pages, can you tell whether the document seems to be something of a chronological report talking about events roughly but continuing on from day-to-day, not every day, but in a chronological fashion of the events during this time? If the registry can assist you however possible, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it's part of a general report of the -- of the group. I think that in there, in the whole report, I do not recall the precise structure or nature, but it could have been done in chronological order or in terms of dates, but probably the chronological order is what is being followed here, but also in terms of areas, that is the area of Mostar. Maybe another one in relation to Jablanica. I would have to actually see the whole report to be able to determine which order it was followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could continue to direct your attention for the moment then to page 34 of the Spanish version, and page 3 of the English translation. I think the Spanish reference may not be correct. Well, yes it is. Given the numbering, it would be page 34 as we were talking about earlier. Page 3 of the English version. If you can find the entry, it says: "The situation is degenerating very rapidly. It comes to a head on May 9th, the date which may be considered as the start of all the hostilities between the HVO and BiH units." Do you see that? I think it's -- yes. The top of that page, sir. Do you -- the second entry on that page, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If you can go down to the third paragraph below that, I believe, the paragraph -- if we can scroll down a bit more on the Spanish version, please. Okay. Thank you. In that paragraph, let's -- starting "La Compania de SpaBat ..." in that paragraph, is that again a reference to the fact that at that time the SpaBat company which was in Mostar was, as it says here, "However, at 1200B --" which I'll ask you about in a moment. "However, at 1200B at the request of the HVO, they are compelled to leave the city." Do you see that? What is the reference --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What is the reference in military jargon, if you will, to 1200B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was going to ask you. I'm not really sure what you mean by 12B. It is not military terminology that we used. Maybe it's an error in the mistake -- it's an error in the report or a mistake in the report. Maybe it's in relation to the -- that 1200B, I don't know exactly what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me see -- make sure that I haven't directed you to the wrong portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Spanish, if you look at the sentence which starts with "Pero es ..." isn't one saying here around 12.00 at the request of the HVO, we need to leave the city? Don't you think it's a typing error here or something that hasn't been spelled properly? Don't you think that's what it should read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That could very well be the case. If I read the report I am to understand that, that at 12.00 noon -- I wouldn't add the B, I wouldn't take regard of the B -- maybe the HVO tells the Spanish Battalion to abandon the city. If I am to read the report, I would understand it in that way. But I don't really know what that B may refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the B shouldn't be in there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It could very well be an error. I'm not really sure. I'm sorry, I'm unable to clarify that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, back to you. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. This is evidently, we now realise, a document that has been translated only in part, 33 to 45, and it's been adduced only in part, but if we don't see what it's a part of, if we don't see the first part of the document, it's hard to talk about this part. It may be dealing with only a certain type of event, but we do not know if it can be tendered unless it's entire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we've understood that. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just before we leave this particular document, on page 4 of the English version -- let me see if I can give you a reference point in the Spanish. Well, several paragraphs down from the one we were just at, in fact. Skip one paragraph and there's another paragraph which should start: "A fact which renders even more difficult the freedom and facility of movement..." If you can see that, sir. I think I can see it there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can actually see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you just quickly tell the Judges what you recall, if anything, or what the Spanish Battalion learned around this time of the destruction of the Bijeli bridge between Mostar and Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot clarify anything further than what is being reported in the document. On the 3rd of May, we found out that the bridge had been blown up and that we couldn't follow the main route in terms of humanitarian aid, and we had to actually search for alternative routes since the bridge was no longer available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At that particular time do you -- can you give us any assistance as to whether that information would have been reported by the Spanish element in Jablanica or was it coming from some Spanish element operating out of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that clearly, but I think that it was one of our vehicles that was going in the direction to Jablanica bordering Mostar as it couldn't come through Mostar and realised that the bridge had blown up -- had been blown up. So I don't know exactly how we found out or how we came to find out of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, there's been a reference in the trial to a temporary road, detour, around the bridge being built. Would the Spanish Battalion have anything to do with building the road that then detoured around, contoured around the geography to replace the bridge that had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Obviously we couldn't use it. We had to use alternative routes. And there were tracks that were already there and perhaps the SpaBat members had to perform some minor repair but there were tracks that were already there. So instead of using the main road we had to use secondary roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Changing -- I want to change the topic, sir, to at the end of -- at the end of June of 1993, around the 30th of June, 1993, there was an attack by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the government forces, on the northern camp or northern barracks area of Mostar. Using that as a time mark, can you tell the Judges what happened after that in connection with being able to gain access or provide humanitarian aid into East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm trying to see the report. I'm trying to remember whether it actually had an impact on the humanitarian aid. I think it was a combat between the two areas, and perhaps the checkpoints had been further reinforced and strengthened, and I think that this could have created further difficulties for our movement but I don't think it had an impact on the attack on this camp in relation to humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask the question differently. Did there come a time in mid-1993 that East Mostar was completely cut off from the Spanish Battalion or any other international organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mostar was completely isolated. The Muslim area was completely isolated and we had physical contact with them, but I would have to check the actual dates, but we spent, I believe, a period of a month, a month and a half without any contact, that is in relation to the Spanish Battalion and the Muslim area of Mostar. We only had radio contact with the area of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. There is -- I have to say there is no way that I would be able to finish today. I think you can observe that it's been a bit slow going, but I know there are some other matters that need to be addressed before the witness is excused. For instance, I need to schedule a time for return because in particular special arrangements have to be made with the translation service as to when they can next arrange for Spanish interpretation, and of course now that -- I'm not able to speak with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So if I understood you correctly, you would like to resume with the examination-in-chief at a later stage, which would be the wisest solution of all, I think. And just before the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that we would have a degree of continuity. I see Mr. Murphy nodding. I think that would be the best solution. You could then supply us with those missing documents. I also have another question to put to you. You gave us a 16-page document with a list of all the exhibits. I assume that at the end of the examination-in-chief you will ask to have all these documents tendered into evidence even if some of these documents were not shown to the witness. But as the witness was a member of the Spanish Battalion, he could authenticate all these exhibits. Is that how you intend to proceed, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, exactly right. At the end of my -- what I had put at the end of my outline, if you will, was to have Mr. -- have the witness, excuse me, confirm that he had, just as we did with these similar exercise previously, to confirm that he had reviewed the full collection of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... prepared to do that. If I might add, Your Honour, in terms of scheduling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- I did raise the possibility because that I knew at least the cross-examination would have to be scheduled, and I did take the liberty in speaking with the witness the other day whether he would be available in the second half of August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- and I believe, if I understood correctly, that he would be available during that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We'll see to that. But before talking about dates, let's see what can be done. We will have to set a date and then the witness can return. You then resume the examination-in-chief because, according to my calculation, you have had two hours and 20 minutes, I think, so far. We shall look into this I think you have probably got an hour and a half or two hours left. So once you will have finished, and there will be a break and we will hand over the documents to the witness and the witness will check all the documents that are in this list, and he will confirm that all of these documents are Spanish Battalion documents, and he will say then that all these documents I have seen are documents that come from my military unit, and then we will start the cross-examination. So we have understood and you have understood that your testimony will resume in a few weeks' time. We had envisaged the end of the month of August. I know that that's a holiday period in Spain at that time. Perhaps you have made your own arrangements for that time, which would be quite understandable. Is there a moment in time which would suit you and suit the Bench, because you will have to come back. We will need to have you here for two or three days. Is there a date you can give us offhand today or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have any problems in any dates that you may wish to propose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we ask you to come back at the end of August, that's all right, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. So, Mr. Scott, what kind of date did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry, there was a problem with translation for a moment. I'm not going to mention other names in front of the witness, this witness, of course, but as you know, we have a witness scheduled for the 17th of August, and we also then have another witness scheduled to return on the 21st of August. So it seems to me that the next available date, if it works for the witness, would be the week of the 28th, the week beginning the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the 28th of August is a Monday. So please make the necessary arrangements to be able to come back on the 28th of August. And the registry will look after that. So that will be the 28th, the 29th, and maybe the 30th as well. In the month of August the weather is usually fine in The Hague. It's not as hot as in Spain, admittedly, but it will be a very pleasant moment. So please make your arrangements so that you can be back on the 28th, the 29th, and 30th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, you must not talk to the Prosecution nor to the Defence counsel nor to the Bench, and if you come across somebody on a beach, don't discuss these matters with him or her. You are not allowed to talk to anybody about all this. Have you understood me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perfectly so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I shall ask the usher to escort you out of the -- out of the courtroom, but please lower the blinds. It's all right now. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, what about next week? Can we move into private session? I think we are still in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're currently in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are currently in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor, Mr. Scott, in open session, to let us know what the schedule is for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was only hesitating because -- whether the names should be mentioned in open session, but I don't think there's -- I don't think there's any issue about it with these two witnesses. Next week, Your Honour, Mr. Kljujic should be arriving and should be available to begin testifying at 2.15 on Monday. He is the only witness scheduled for next week. I understand that next week is a three-day week because of the Plenary is my -- am I correct on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On Thursday we have the Plenary for the Judges, so we will be sitting on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday. That's fine. So having nothing more on the agenda for today, I would like to ask you to come back at 2.15 for the people concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have the -- a word for just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, usually when the Judges have stood up, that means that the Court stands adjourned, but what would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had mentioned that I wanted -- wished to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. I had completely forgotten about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to object to the tendering into evidence of the documents mentioned by the witness, yesterday's witness, Mr. Hujdur. I -- we are going to be filing a request on Monday. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're talking about the documents that have been filed by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they have been given an exhibit number, so you would like this number to be withdrawn; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They have -- these documents have been given a number, but I don't think you've rendered a decision, I don't think you have said whether yes or no these could be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you check this out, please, because if I remember correctly -- the registrar has just confirmed that this has not been done. So you are going to file a written submission or are you going to make an oral submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall continue in English. It will be more efficient. [In English] Mr. President, the Prosecution -- Your Honour -- in writing regarding documents that had been, I think, produced or identified by the witness, Mr. Beese, and in response to that, we indicated that we would like to make a written response. The Trial Chamber agreed that that would be appropriate, and that response is nearly complete. We hope to file it on Monday. And it will indicate our submissions not only about those documents but also matters of more general principle regarding the way in which the Trial Chamber should approach the question of admissibility. And briefly stated, I think the difference between the two sides is that we would contend that there is a judicial function important to -- to go through before the documents are admitted and not simply afterwards in assessing their weight. In relation to the documents produced by yesterday's witness, Mr. Hujdur, Your Honours will recall that these documents were reports which he said had been issued by the commission or body of which he became a member, dealing with damage to property and other similar matters, and Your Honours raised the question of why they had not been signed. The witness indicated, I think, that he had been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In one case a report on the destruction of houses, P 015764, we established that there was annex missing which may have been of some importance and generally there was just no indication of where the information came from, how many levels of hearsay were involved in compiling it, and, Your Honour, it is our position that the Trial Chamber could legitimately have a reservation about even accepting these documents because of their low probative value, and because under Rule 89 you are able to consider whether the demands of a fair trial outweigh a low probative value. And the Trial Chamber may also request verification of the authenticity of these documents. And all of these subjects, Your Honour, will be addressed in more detail in our written memorandum. I would simply ask that the Court take note of our objection and consider it in conjunction with those written submissions that we will make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall give the floor to Mr. Scott so that he can respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, only very short for now. I just -- as was -- as came up this morning already, some of these issues keep coming up and they are indeed quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- and no one says to the contrary, but I suggest that now is not the time to get into a lengthy dialogue on this particular topic. My only comment for today is this: I invite the Chamber, if it will assist the Chamber, and of course the Chamber will decide, but if it would assist the Chamber that there indeed be a more deliberate discussion or hearing specifically on these matters, not in two minutes when everybody wants to leave the courtroom, let me just say this, though: I just -- we are not writing here, and I think the Chamber knows, we are not writing here on a completely clean slate. Anyone of us who were to start the ICTY over again might or might not design a different set of rules, but there is an established jurisprudence and there is a set of practice that has been followed here for approximately the past 12 years or so. And there is a reason for that. There is a reason that the rules and the practices are what they are, and we'll certainly ask the Chamber to be mindful of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All of this will be settled by a written decision. We were supposed to render a written decision relating to Witness Beese, which is in progress, so please make your written filings, the Prosecution will respond, and we shall render our decision. As far as I'm concerned, I felt that this had already been settled because we'd set guidelines in an order which had been rendered at the beginning of the trial, so we shall respond in writing. It is now 2.00, and we're going to have a 30-minute break. I need to move back into private session, Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are currently back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in open session the Court stands adjourned for today, and I would like to ask all of you to come back for our next hearing, which will be on Monday at a quarter past two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of June, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.00 p.m.,
